summary:
Santa Catarina stands under Brazil's national framework, and its own record shows a state legislature moving against trans and LGBTIQ people while the courts have narrowed the state's own protections.

The state constitution carries an anti-discrimination clause dating to 2002 that lists sexual orientation among the protected grounds, but as of 2019 it does not address discrimination against transgender people. Two state statutes that did cover gender identity have been stripped back: State Law No. 12,534 of 4 April 2003 was repealed on 8 October 2015 by Complementary Law No. 656, and Complementary Law No. 527 of 28 December 2010 was partially overturned on 11 October 2018 after a 2015 Supreme Federal Court challenge on labour-law grounds. What remains of Complementary Law No. 527 penalises private entities and, where applicable, state public servants who promote, permit or tolerate discriminatory acts based on gender or sexual orientation, covering violent, coercive or vexatious acts, refusal of entry to places of free public access, denial or surcharging of lodging and property transactions, and prohibition of affectionate expression permitted to others, punishable by a R$2,500 fine rising to R$5,000 on repeat, a 30-day licence suspension or revocation, and up to 30 days' suspension for state servants; complaints go to the State Secretariat of Public Security and Defense of the Citizen, with fines paid into the State Civil Police Improvement Fund. In ADI 5307 on 29 October 2018 the Supreme Federal Court unanimously declared Article 2, items VI and VII of that law formally unconstitutional.

Legislative hostility is documented in volume. From January 2019 to June 2025, state deputies introduced 19 anti-LGBTQIA+ bills against 4 pro-LGBTQIA+ bills, including proposals to prohibit neutral language in official government communications and to bar minors from hormone therapy, surgical interventions and other gender-transition care; 4 of the anti-LGBTQIA+ bills were archived and none were enacted. As of 2025 the Legislative Assembly had 19 anti-LGBTQ bills on record with 11 authored by the Liberal Party. A 2026 count recorded 271 unconstitutional laws processed since 2015 against women's or LGBTQ rights, about 70% involving the trans and travesti community and 41% ruled unconstitutional by the Supreme Federal Court. A separate report covering January 2015 to October 2025 found the Legislative Assembly and its 295 municipal chambers approved or advanced at least 271 laws, bills and normative acts already declared unconstitutional by the Supreme Federal Court, 41% attacking gender and sexuality with particular focus on LGBTIA+ people, 36% already in force and only 11% judicially annulled, concentrated in the Vale do Itajaí and accelerating in the last five years.

Restroom access is contested. On 21 January 2026 Governor Jorginho Mello signed State Law No. 19,686/2026 requiring all public and private educational institutions from preschool through higher and vocational education to maintain strictly separate male and female restrooms and changing rooms; from 18 June 2026 the Federal University of Santa Catarina installed signs indicating restrooms may be used in accordance with gender identity. In a 2014 Florianópolis shopping-mall case where a trans woman was denied access to the women's restroom, a lower court ordered R$15,000 in compensation for pain and suffering, the Court of Justice of Santa Catarina overturned it, and on 6 June 2024 the Supreme Federal Court dismissed her appeal pending since 2014 by an 8-3 vote, withdrawing its recognized general repercussion on procedural grounds that the original claim pleaded only consumer-law damages rather than constitutional provisions, thereby issuing no binding constitutional ruling on trans bathroom access; in August 2025 an extraordinary appeal was filed with the Inter-American Court of Human Rights against both courts.

Education policy has also been restricted. A decree of Governor Carlos Moises on 15 June 2021 banned gender-neutral language in state schools until it was overturned on 6 May 2025 by the Supreme Federal Court, and a Joinville law of 20 December 2021 banned it in public office until struck down on 3 August 2022 by the Court of Justice. On 15 October 2025 the Supreme Federal Court struck down a 2015 Tubarão law that had prohibited teaching of gender and sexual orientation in schools. On 1 April 2026 Governor Jorginho Mello signed a law published 6 April allowing parents to prohibit children from participating in classes on LGBTQ topics. In December 2023 the Constitution and Justice Committee of the Legislative Assembly approved a bill prohibiting transgender women from participating in women's sports, still under review as of 18 August 2026.

Document and registry practice in the state runs through the courts rather than a state statute. Since 2020 people in Santa Catarina have obtained documents recording non-binary gender through the courts or notarial offices, although no specific state law prescribes this; in 2021 Idris Kawabe became the first person in Santa Catarina to judicially change documents to reflect a neutral gender, and judicial actions are still required because no state law recognizes the marker, with legal sex still required on birth certificates. The Army provides that any person in the draft cohort expressing a gender identity other than male who holds a final, unappealable court ruling or civil registry amendment is treated as non-binary in the same manner as intersex individuals and considered exempt from mandatory military service for not meeting Federal Constitution, Military Service Law, implementing regulations and the 2024 General Conscription Plan requirements.

Violence and hostility figures for the state are recorded. In 2024 three murders of trans people were recorded in Santa Catarina. The 2024 Brazilian Public Security Yearbook reported 85 cases of intentional bodily injury against LGBTQ individuals in the state, with low rates attributed to underreporting. On 3 September 2026 the Court of Justice ordered the parents of a gay teenager in Jaguaruna to pay R$100,000 in compensation after kicking him out and exposing his sexual orientation on social media.

Florianópolis carries some protective signals. A legal guide updated 5 April 2026 names it among Brazil's broadly welcoming major cities, with active LGBTQ+ communities, pride events and legal infrastructure accustomed to processing same-sex marriages, adoptions and name or gender-marker changes, while smaller cities and rural areas may present more social friction even though legal rights are identical nationwide. In a Florianópolis case, judge M. C. F. Ribeiro da Silva of the 1st Civil Court blocked immigration authorities from deporting an Italian citizen who had lived over ten years in a stable relationship with a lesbian Brazilian. On 29 April 2013 the Corregedoria-Geral da Justiça of Santa Catarina authorized notarial and civil-registry offices to process marriage habilitations regardless of the sex of the spouses, allowing same-sex couples where both partners reside in Santa Catarina to formalize civil marriage and expanding Article 629 of the CGJ Code of Norms beyond the stable union recognized since 2011.
tangentialFactors:
The 2026 count of 271 unconstitutional laws processed since 2015 is a raw count for Santa Catarina alone, not a per-capita comparison with other states; the same applies to the 19 anti-LGBTQ bills recorded as of 2025 and the 19-versus-4 bill tally from January 2019 to June 2025. The 85 cases of intentional bodily injury reported by the 2024 Brazilian Public Security Yearbook are described by the source itself as low because of underreporting, so the figure understates rather than measures incidence.

State-level restrictions sit against a national backdrop that is more protective: the Supreme Federal Court's 2018 ADI 4275 ruling allows alteration of name and gender in the civil registry without surgery or judicial authorization, ADO 26 and MI 4733 equate transphobia and homophobia to the crime of racism until Congress legislates, ADPF 527 requires reasoned judicial placement of transgender women prisoners, and ADPF 787 requires the Unified Health System to guarantee trans and travesti people full access to health services. A deeply conservative Congress has nonetheless generated a surge of anti-LGBTIQ proposals nationally, including efforts to repeal marriage equality recognized in 2013.

In September 2025 the federal government reinstated the National LGBTI+ Health Technical Committee, a participatory mechanism dissolved in 2019, for shaping and monitoring inclusive public-health policy. The Superior Court of Justice has ruled that nonbinary people may amend their civil registry to reflect their gender identity, and foreign same-sex spouses and partners are treated identically for visa and residence categories, including the spousal residence permit, with foreign same-sex marriages recognised for immigration purposes. Joint and second-parent adoption is confirmed by STF RE 846.102 (2015), and gender-marker changes proceed without surgery.
localsOnly:
State Law No. 19,686/2026, signed on 21 January 2026, binds public and private educational institutions from preschool through higher and vocational education to maintain strictly separate male and female restrooms and changing rooms. The Federal University of Santa Catarina's contrary signage from 18 June 2026 is an institutional practice, not a repeal of the state law.

The law signed 1 April 2026 and published 6 April 2026 lets parents prohibit children from participating in classes on LGBTQ topics. The December 2023 bill barring transgender women from women's sports remains before the Legislative Assembly's Constitution and Justice Committee, under review as of 18 August 2026.

Complementary Law No. 527 remains the operative state complaint mechanism for discrimination based on gender or sexual orientation by private entities and state servants, with complaints lodged at the State Secretariat of Public Security and Defense of the Citizen and fines directed to the State Civil Police Improvement Fund, though Article 2, items VI and VII were struck in ADI 5307 on 29 October 2018. Non-binary document changes require a court or notarial action because no state statute provides for them.
outOfScopeNotes:
The source inventory does not resolve whether State Law No. 19,686/2026 has been challenged in court or how institutions have complied beyond the Federal University of Santa Catarina signage. The status of the December 2023 sports bill after 18 August 2026 is not documented here.

The 2024 figure of three recorded murders of trans people in Santa Catarina is a raw count without a population denominator, and the inventory provides no state general homicide rate against which to compare it; the 85 bodily-injury cases likewise carry no denominator. Whether the 2026 count of 271 unconstitutional laws and the January 2015 to October 2025 report's 271 acts are the same dataset is not stated by the sources.

Whether the Inter-American Court of Human Rights appeal filed in August 2025 in the Florianópolis restroom case has produced any ruling is not documented in this inventory.
